title: Leading Through a Hard Season Without Losing Yourself 2026
author: Josh Gratsch
summary: Josh Gratsch looks back four years to a cash-flow crisis months into his tenure as CEO, when he cut staff before the holidays and the company needed eighteen months to recover. His central belief is that a hard season may require you to change how you lead but does not have to change who you are. He admits he compartmentalised emotion and treated culture and business as a choice, when the team actually needed transparency about the current position, clarity on next steps and confidence in working together. He describes a pragmatic optimism that acknowledges difficulty without pretending, and he stresses that people cope better when they know the why, share ownership and feel respected. Tactically he would shrink planning to the smallest meaningful weekly steps, shift from quarterly to weekly cadence and lean on a personal board of advisors. He closes with three steps: acknowledge reality, be transparent, and make the path visible.
points: A hard season may require you to change how you lead, but it does not have to change who you are.
Teams need not certainty but honest transparency, clear next steps and a pragmatic optimism that admits the difficulty.
Culture and business are not a trade-off: trust built through consistent leadership was critical to rebuilding the company.
In a crisis, shrink planning to the smallest meaningful steps for the week and run a weekly operating cadence in place of quarterly planning.
Surround yourself with trusted advisors of varied backgrounds, since a leader under pressure is prone to rash decisions.
quotes: A hard season may require you to change how you lead. It doesn’t have to change who you are.
But looking back, I can see that focusing on the business alone wasn’t enough to give my team confidence that we could pull ourselves out of the nose-dive we found ourselves in.

I couldn’t give them certainty about the future. But I could give them transparency about our current position, clarity on what we'd do next, and confidence that if we worked together, we’d increase our chances of a positive outcome.
They needed a pragmatic form of optimism; one that acknowledges the challenges while not losing sight of the belief that things can improve.

People are better able to navigate these situations when a) they know the “why,” b) they’re given ownership to be a part of the solution, and c) they’re treated with respect and trust that someone has their back.

Lastly, we can adjust how we operate as leaders while not compromising our character. The instant we negate our values and principles for the sake of the business, we begin to lose trust. When we lose trust, we lose our team.
What are the smallest meaningful steps we can take this week to create measurable progress?
Quarterly planning becomes less relevant. A weekly operating cadence is much more palatable when unknowns are amplified.
